description: TrendWatt turns any point on Earth into an evidence-backed energy trend report: 35 years of NASA POWER data, six energy-relevant variables, Mann–Kendall significance tests and Theil–Sen slopes, confidence tiers, and sub-period robustness checks — each trend translated into a grid-planning implication with stated assumptions. It even flags its own fragile headlines. For planners, telling signal from noise is the product.
summary:
TrendWatt provides one solution for any point on Earth: "Is my energy resource changing — or is it noise?" Pick a location and the app pulls 35 years of NASA POWER data, applies Mann–Kendall significance testing with Theil–Sen slope estimation to six energy-relevant variables, and translates each result into a grid-planning implication with stated assumptions.
It meets the challenge directly: selecting mission-derived variables, visualizing multi-decade time series for a chosen region, quantifying the rate of change, and testing significance — then going further with confidence tiers (HIGH / FRAGILE / INCONCLUSIVE) and sub-period robustness checks. Across four test sites, Phoenix shows +19.3% (HIGH), two findings are deliberately reported INCONCLUSIVE, and Jodhpur's −8.8% headline was auto-flagged FRAGILE at the 2001 sensor boundary, yet persisted in the single-sensor era (p<0.0001). The tool caught its own headline — and the risk survived.
This matters because grid planners commit decades of infrastructure to resource assumptions. TrendWatt makes those assumptions testable and auditable: telling signal from noise is the product. Roadmap: GRACE-FO hydrology, wind power density, and portfolio screening.
details:
1. What does it do or how does it work?
TrendWatt answers one question for any location on Earth: is my energy resource actually changing — or is it noise? It turns 35 years of NASA Earth observations into significance-tested trends, translated into energy-planning decisions.
How it works:
1.
Select a location — four showcase sites or any custom coordinate.
2.
Fetch NASA POWER monthly data (1990–2024) for six energy-relevant variables: cooling degree days, heating degree days, solar irradiance, 50 m wind speed, precipitation, and temperature. No API key required.
3.
Extract annual series directly from POWER's month-"13" annual aggregates.
4.
Test significance with a tie-corrected Mann–Kendall test (α = 0.05) and Theil–Sen slopes; assign confidence tiers (HIGH / MODERATE / WATCH / INCONCLUSIVE).
5.
Stress-test the trend with a sub-period robustness check; the solar record is split at 2001 to handle the GEWEX-SRB → CERES sensor transition.
6.
Translate to decisions — e.g., cooling-demand growth, PV yield erosion, wind power-density change — with every assumption stated inline.
7.
Export a Planner Brief: a one-page, hash-reproducible summary with the exact API request, data hash, timestamp, and limitations.
Real results: Phoenix cooling demand +19.3% (p<0.0001); Rajasthan solar irradiance −8.8%, flagged as sensor-transition-fragile yet confirmed at −8.8% within the single-sensor era (p<0.0001); German Bight wind and Brazilian hydro rainfall correctly labeled INCONCLUSIVE. The app runs from cached data, so the demo never depends on live connectivity.


2. What benefits does it have?
Decision-ready output: planners get implications (peak-load sensitivity, PV yield derating, water-stress screening), not just charts.
Protection against noise: inconclusive trends are labeled plainly, so users don't act on signals the record can't support — two of our four showcase findings are deliberately inconclusive.
Scientific defensibility: recognized non-parametric tests, confidence tiers, artifact checks, and stated assumptions stand up to technical review.
Reproducibility: every result regenerates from an embedded data hash and exact request URL — auditable by anyone.
Accessible and free: open NASA data, no API key, open-source zero-dependency statistical core — usable by a small utility in a developing grid as easily as a major developer.
Fast screening: a defensible first pass in minutes, before committing to expensive site-specific studies.


3. What is the intended impact of the project?
Energy infrastructure built today will operate for 25–40 years under a changing climate, yet planning still leans on historical averages that assume the past predicts the future. TrendWatt's intended impact is to make climate non-stationarity visible and actionable at the point where energy decisions are made — siting, capacity planning, yield assumptions, and water-stress triage.
By distinguishing real trends from noise, it helps avoid two costly errors: under-preparing for genuine shifts (rising cooling load, eroding solar resource) and over-reacting to variability that isn't a trend. Because it is free, open, and globally applicable, it democratizes rigorous climate screening for underserved grids and communities. More broadly, it builds statistical literacy: showing what is changing, where, how much, and whether it is significant — exactly the challenge's mandate — in language planners and the public can act on.


4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?
Language: Python 3.10+. Statistical core: pure standard library (urllib, math, hashlib, collections) — Mann–Kendall and Theil–Sen implemented and validated directly. Interface: Streamlit + Plotly; pandas for data handling. Data: NASA POWER Monthly Point API (community=RE). Version control & deployment: GitHub; Streamlit Community Cloud. Hardware: standard laptop; no specialized hardware required.


5. How is your project creative?
Most trend tools stop at "the line goes up." TrendWatt's creativity is in what happens after detection:
Energy translation layer: the same statistics become cooling demand, PV yield, wind power density, and water availability — the variables decisions are actually made on.
Honesty as a feature: INCONCLUSIVE is a first-class verdict. We show where the data cannot support a decision, which most dashboards hide.
Self-skepticism: the sub-period check caught our own headline — Rajasthan's −8.8% spans a sensor transition — then confirmed the risk survives in the homogeneous era. The tool audits itself.
Decision artifact, not visualization: the Planner Brief carries provenance (hash, exact request, timestamp) so any finding can be regenerated and defended.
The creative leap is treating confidence and reproducibility as the product, not the plot.


6. What factors did your team consider?
Statistical validity: seasonality (handled via annual aggregation), tied values (tie-corrected variance), outliers (Theil–Sen robustness), and the limits of short sub-periods (sign-consistency check, not significance claims).
Data homogeneity: POWER's solar record changes source in 2001; we split there rather than let a sensor transition masquerade as climate trend.
Physical meaning: precipitation is a water-availability indicator, not streamflow; wind uses a cube-of-mean proxy; temperature is reported in absolute °C, never meaningless percentages.
Resolution and scope: ~50–100 km source resolution means screening-level triage, not site micrometeorology — stated explicitly so the tool is never overclaimed.
Reliability under demo conditions: cache-first design so the app works offline; live fetch is optional.
Reproducibility and credit: embedded hashes and exact requests; full NASA POWER attribution; open-source licensing.
Scope discipline: a 48-hour build demanded freezing features early — four sites, six variables, one export — rather than over-reaching.
